## Big Idea

- Pick up where [Regional Curves](11RegionalCurves.qmd) left off. RCS lifts the segment-length curse by fitting one curve to the whole collection, and pays for it in assumptions. Signal-free goes the other way: keep a curve for each tree, but stop that curve from bending to the climate.
- The problem it answers is trend distortion [@melvin2008, p. 72-74]: a curve fitted to a tree's widths can't tell age from a run of good or bad years near the end of the series, so it bends toward them and the indices lose part of the run. Where many series end in the same years, as in any living collection, the bends line up and the chronology's recent end is distorted.
- The idea: if the chronology is the common signal, dividing each tree's widths by it leaves "signal-free" widths, which are what the tree would have grown in an average year. Fit the curve to those, divide the real widths by that curve, and repeat until the chronology stops changing [@melvin2008, p. 74-75].
- What it can't do, said up front, in their words: chronologies still come out with an arbitrary slope, so signal-free leaves the segment-length curse in place [@melvin2008, abstract and p. 85].
- Promise: by the end you can run `ssf`, read what each iteration did, and know which part of the chronology to be wary of.

## Packages

- `dplR` and `ggplot2`, the simulation from [chapter 2](02CoresToRecord.qmd), and `makeClimate` from [Detrending](08Detrending.qmd). `cowplot` if the loop figure needs stacked panels.
- Data: `wa082`, with its 1900 gap filled (`ssf` stops on an internal `NA`). `ca533` (Campito Mountain bristlecone, `recode.zeros = TRUE`). Say in a sentence why not `co021` and `gp.rwl`; see When It Stops.

## Trend Distortion

- Rebuild @melvin2008's Fig. 1 on one simulated series: a straight-line decline in width, then a 20-year growth increase of 20% near the end. Fit a line with and without the increase. The difference between the two sets of indices is the distortion, a wedge that grows toward the end of the series (p. 73-74).
- Then on a stand: the chronology from spline curves against the true one, at the recent end. The simulation knows the age trend, so the distortion can be measured, not argued.
- Why only the ends matter much: in the middle of a long chronology the bends fall in different years in different trees and average out (p. 72-73).

## The Loop

- @melvin2008's steps (p. 75), each with the line of `ssf` that does it:
  1. Detrend and build a chronology.
  2. Divide each series by the chronology: the signal-free widths.
  3. Put each signal-free series back on the mean of its widths.
  4. In years with only one series, keep the measured width (a chronology of one tree is that tree).
  5. Fit a curve to each signal-free series.
  6. Divide the measured widths by those curves.
  7. Average into a new chronology.
  8. Repeat 2 to 7 until the chronology stops changing.
- On Hurricane Ridge: `ssf(..., return.info = TRUE)` keeps every iteration. It stops after 8 iterations. The first and last chronologies correlate 0.98 year to year and 0.92 after a 31-year running mean; the running mean's SD goes from 0.047 to 0.065. Show the iterations as the 2024 chapter did (a series and its curves, the chronologies one over another, the animation if it's worth its weight).
- The stopping rule: `ssf` high-pass filters each chronology (a spline at the median series length), takes the median absolute difference from the last one, weighted by sample depth, and stops below 0.0005 (`mad.threshold`). @melvin2008 used the mean absolute difference of the high-pass filtered difference, at the same 0.0005 (p. 75); CRUST stops at 0.0001 (`cur_detrend` in `stand.f90`). Hurricane Ridge: 0.0021 after the second iteration, 0.0004 at the eighth. For comparison, @BriffaMelvin2011 describe the RCS form as stopping when every value of the signal-free chronology is within 1.0 ± 0.002, with the leftover variance falling to about 20% of its previous value at each pass, so usually four or five iterations (appendix, p. 143).
- Say what the rule ignores: it looks only at the high-pass part, on purpose, because the low-frequency part has no single answer (their limitation 3, p. 75). That is why the recent end needs a second look (Reading the Recent End).

## What It Recovers

- One small run, not a table of methods: the segment-length experiment from 08 and 11 with `Spline` and `ssf` only, against dividing by the true age trend. On 100 stands with 80-year swings, `ssf` kept 57% of the slow swing and `Spline` 27% (correlations of the 31-year running means with the climate's, 0.66 and 0.63). The draft can use fewer stands.
- RCS from chapter 11 kept 86 to 88%, on its own assumptions. One sentence.

## Reading the Recent End

- No bias tables here. @melvin2008 say signal-free chronologies still have an arbitrary slope and that whether their last half a tree-length should slope up, down or not at all can't be judged with curve-fitting (p. 84). @BriffaMelvin2011 say the same for RCS: even with signal-free, a chronology of living trees has a "largely 'arbitrary'" slope (p. 129). The stopping rule only looks at high frequencies, so it says nothing about the slow part of the recent end either.
- Point to the work in progress: what signal-free does to the recent end, across climates and settings, is the subject of a paper from @Wilce2024's thesis (Wilce, Bunn, Anchukaitis and Swetnam, in preparation; check the author list and wording with Andy). Two or three sentences, no numbers from the scratch runs.
- Revisit when the paper is out: cite its results here, and whatever it settles about how `ssf` rescales.

## When It Stops

- `ssf` refuses rather than guess, and the messages say why. On the book's data:
  - `wa082` as read: an internal `NA` (1900). Fill it first, as in [Detrending](08Detrending.qmd).
  - `ca533`: in 645 only one series is present and its ring is zero, so the chronology is zero there (error [4]). `recode.zeros = TRUE` runs it.
  - `gp.rwl`: at iteration 1, curves for tree 10 go below zero in 1990 (error [1]).
  - `co021`: error [1] at iteration 12, curves for 642244 and 646211 below zero. Mesa Verde has many absent rings, and dividing by a chronology near zero makes huge signal-free values.
- @melvin2008's own guards: curves never below zero, iterations limited by replication when the curve type can change, and a minimum spline value of 0.01 mm (p. 75, 84). CRUST floors every curve at 0.02 mm instead of stopping. Point out that `ssf` stops instead, and that the reader can see why in the message.

## Hurricane Ridge and Campito

- Two real collections, standard spline chronology against `ssf`, as 31-year running means for years with 10 or more cores.
- Hurricane Ridge (1770 to 1983 with 10 or more cores): little changes. The last 50 years minus the rest go from -0.005 to -0.018.
- Campito (1037 to 1983): the running mean's SD goes from 0.112 to 0.126, and the last 50 years minus the rest from +0.025 to +0.151. Is that late rise growth or something the method made? Nothing in the widths alone separates the two. Say so, as 11 did for Gus Pearson. Nothing about bristlecone growth history goes in without a source read.

## Choosing

- Opinion, mine, with reasons: signal-free helps most where a per-tree curve is the right model and a run of years near the end of many series is the question. It recovers more of the slow climate than the curve alone. Its recent end is the least certain part of it (Reading the Recent End).
- So: run it next to the standard chronology and look at what changed. Agreement between them is evidence of no strong distortion (@melvin2008, p. 82, make this argument for Luosto). A change concentrated at the recent end is the one to distrust, and the one most likely to be reported.
- @melvin2008 recommend RCS, not curve-fitting, for comparing past and recent growth (p. 85). Signal-free RCS [@BriffaMelvin2011, p. 120, 128-129] isn't in dplR. One sentence.

## Wrapping Up

- A curve fitted to a tree bends toward its last few decades; signal-free fits the curve to the widths with the shared signal divided out, and repeats. It gets back more of the slow climate, and its recent end needs the same care as any per-tree chronology's, or more. Smoothing and Filtering next.

## Exercises

- Run `ssf` on Hurricane Ridge with `mad.threshold = 0.001` and `0.0001`. How many iterations does each take, and how much does the last 50 years change?
- Give a simulated stand @melvin2008's step increase (20% from 50 years before the end) and compare `Spline` and `ssf`.
- Run `ssf` on Campito with and without `recode.zeros`. What does the error message say, and which year is the problem?
